title: The wave-2 orchestrator pass loses the project lease and the run stops instead of fanning out again
description:
The last unmet clause of Phase 2's definition of done, and the reason it is unmet is now precise rather than a shrug.

Tick wiy built the every-wave fan-out: after a container wave finishes, a 'wave'-phase orchestrator pass boots, computes the next wave with Go's own wave.Compute inside the sandbox, and asks POST /api/wave for it. That machinery RAN, live, on run_659b7cf253e4462aa6c0dfebbe820ddd — the Workflow instance shows wave:1:killcheck, wave:1:boot, wave:1:lease, wave:1:wait, wave:1:watch, wave:1:revoke. So the pass is real and reached.

It then failed on the first thing it needed:

  wave:1:boot:1-1    {"process_id":"proc_1787449861245_9gnerx"}
  wave:1:lease:1-1   {"ok":false}
  wave:1:watch:1:0-1 {"trip":{"kind":"stop","hard":true,"detail":"the dispatch lease was lost to another run"}}
  wave:1:revoke:1-1  {"revoked":1}

Fifteen seconds from boot to hard stop. The pass never got to compute a wave, so no second container wave was ever requested, and the run went to closeout.

WHAT TO WORK OUT FIRST, because the message may be lying about the cause. 'lost to another run' is what the code says when leaseStatus() does not name this run. Two very different situations produce that, and they need opposite fixes:
1. The lease genuinely expired between the end of the container wave and the boot of the wave pass. The lease record on an earlier run showed a 10-minute expiry; a container wave now runs 60-90 minutes, and the legs that watch it are supervisor-side. If nothing renews the lease across a long wave, expiry is near-certain rather than a race — and then the message is misleading, because nobody took it, it simply lapsed.
2. Some other run really did acquire it. run_f7bd5a36 was still in 'stopping' when this run started, and this epic has repeatedly produced runs that never reach a terminal state. If a stale run can take or hold the lease, that is the bug.

Determine which before changing anything. The evidence to settle it is in the RunRoom's lease record and the run index — read them rather than reasoning from the message.

Note the interaction with wiy's design, which is otherwise right: it deliberately made POST /api/wave VERIFY the lease rather than acquire one, so an in-run orchestrator can never take a second lease. That is correct and must survive the fix. The gap is that nothing keeps the lease alive on the run's behalf while its containers work — the verification is sound and the thing being verified went stale under it.

Also fix the message if cause 1 is what happened: 'the dispatch lease was lost to another run' should not be what an operator reads when the lease simply expired. That is the collapse-distinct-failure-classes rule again, which this epic has now hit four times.
acceptance_criteria: A cloud run whose first container wave takes over an hour still holds its project lease when the wave pass boots, and that pass dispatches a second container wave. Proven by a live run showing two dispatch batches. An expired lease and a stolen lease report differently.
